_note: What to generate next, in priority order. `npm run pixellab -- --list` prices a run without spending anything; a run generates every subject that has no sheet yet. Descriptions are THE SUBJECT ONLY — the style anchor carries palette, outline weight, shading and colour count, and a long style suffix actively fights it.
_budget: Pro tools cost 20 generations each against 2,000/month. Check the live figure with get_balance before a batch rather than trusting this line. THE CONCURRENCY LIMIT IS 8 JOBS, not a time window: fire eight, they finish in about nine minutes, fire eight more. There is no cooldown to wait out.
_fieldRule: Anything that reaches the game FIELD must end up 32x32; generate larger and use PixelLab's Unzoom, or generate at 32 directly. Card icons are exempt and 64px is better — a card window zooms by integers and wants the detail.
_next: For directional field art the pipeline is: generate one side view here, then 'Generate 8 rotations', then 'Animate with text' for the walk. Those are separate tools and are not automated by this script yet.

_characterNote: The CHARACTER BUILDER is a separate pipeline from this queue and is not run by `npm run pixellab`. Characters are generated once, get a character id, and are then animated as states of that id -- so a walk, an attack and a death are the same figure rather than three drawings that resemble each other. See docs/PIXELLAB.md. It needs a `pixellabRig` block in art/sprites.json before anything it produces can be packed, and that rig must be written against a real generated sheet rather than guessed from the docs.
_characterWishlist: infected_hen / rooster / hand / hog / sheep -- walk, attack, death. Replaces the CSS-filtered animals.
barn_dog -- walk + bite. Currently a generic feral dog.
whitacre_bull -- walk + charge. The legendary minion, currently a boss sprite.
the Duster and the Prize Bull -- both bosses currently have a walk and nothing else.

_characterRecipe._note: Claude Design's settings for the character builder. Not defaults -- set them by hand. Full write-up and the prompt template in docs/PIXELLAB.md.
promptShape: body itemised, and the POSE stated explicitly -- an action pose cannot be animated into a different one
a line of authorial intent (what the player should read this as)
_characterRecipe.differsFromIcons: Icons take the SUBJECT ONLY; a style suffix fights the anchor. Characters DO carry palette and outline direction, because there is far more surface for the model to drift on.

_apiNote: VALIDATED against the live API on 2026-08-15. Two icons generated end to end and wired in (work_boots, feed_sack) at 20 generations each. Two things worth knowing that the handoff could not have: the style anchor can be passed as `style_image_url` pointing at this repo's own raw.githubusercontent URL, which avoids a 25KB base64 argument entirely -- the repo being public makes it its own asset host. And create_image_pro returns each candidate as a SEPARATE file, not the web UI's 4x4 sheet, so pixellab-cut's `icon` command does not apply; `npm run cut -- single <src> <dst>` was added for that path.
_styleAnchorNote: THE ANCHOR IS A SHEET OF FARM PRODUCE, and with the default style_copy (all four of color_palette, outline, detail, shading) the model copies its SUBJECT as well as its rendering. The first oak came back as four pumpkins and an onion. For anything that is not a small hand-held object, pass style_copy WITHOUT "detail" -- palette, outline and shading carry the look, and detail is what drags the anchor content across. Same prompt, same anchor, detail dropped: a correct oak, first try.
_modelNote: create_image_pro is 20 generations and returns a SET -- 64 candidates at <=42px, 16 at <=85px, 4 at <=170px, 1 above. 64x64 is the sweet spot: 16 candidates for one price, and enough resolution for a card. Going to 128px to get a bigger sprite costs you twelve of the sixteen tries, which is exactly when a bad generation has nowhere to hide. Generate small, draw at an integer zoom. The cheaper models (pixen at 1 generation, pixflux for img2img/forced palette) are the right call for simple flat objects; pro earns its cost on anything with form.
_pickNote: npm run fetch -- <job-id> <name> pulls every candidate plus a 4-across contact sheet into assets/pixellab/sheets/<name>/. Look at the contact sheet, then npm run cut -- single <sheet>/<name>_NN.png assets/pixellab/picked/<name>.png. Keep every candidate: they are paid for, and the first cell picked has more than once not been the best one.

_ranchRoster._note: THE OWNER'S OWN ANIMALS. These are real animals on a real ranch and the point is that the game has them in it. Side views are GENERATED AND STAGED in assets/pixellab/picked/ -- fjord_pony, arabian_horse, draft_mule, donkey, rooster_big. rooster_big is wired (the yard scene). The other four are not wired to anything yet, deliberately: a side view is a reference, not an enemy.
_ranchRoster._whatIsMissing: PACKING AND WIRING. All ten animals are complete as ART -- eight rotations and a nine-frame walk in each of eight directions, in assets/pixellab/object/<name>/. None of it is in the atlas and nothing references it. What is left is engineering, not generation.
_ranchRoster._sizeRule: Field art ends at 32x32. These were generated at 64 for the candidate count; unzoom or regenerate at 32 before packing, and do NOT scale a 64px sprite down in CSS -- it breaks the pixel grid.

_ranchRoster._thenWhat: After the walk: map PixelLab compass (south, south-west, west, north-west, north, north-east, east, south-east) onto the game order. That is a FOURTH direction order in this project after the humanoids, the animals and the tractor -- measure it, do not assume it. Then pack as a directional sheet and add it to art/sprites.json.
_ranchRoster._measuredBy: npm run animal  (tools/animal-check.ts). Re-run it rather than trusting this block; it prints the table and writes tools/animal-check.png at the game's 2x zoom on real grass.
_howToWireIt: DIRECTION MAPPING: MEASURED, AND IT IS NOT A NEW ORDER. south->down, north->up, west->left, east->right -- byte-identical to `compassToDirection` already shipped for the infected farmhand in art/sprites.json. The 'fourth direction order' worry conflated two different problems: the three sheet FAMILIES pack anonymous bands, so which band is which had to be proved; a PixelLab object returns eight files NAMED for their compass points, so there is no order to infer, only names to verify. Verified on all ten by silhouette IoU: south and north are self-symmetric (0.68-1.00), east and west are not (0.26-0.75), and east matches a mirrored west (0.88-1.00). Front and rear views are bilaterally symmetric; profiles are not, and the two profiles mirror each other.

FRAME COUNT: confirmed 8 directions x 9 frames on all ten. LimeZu animals are 6. atlas.json already emits per-sheet clip lengths for exactly this reason, so this is a manifest entry and not a renderer change.

SIZE: the number that matters is the PROFILE, not the face-on view, because that is where the camera height shows. Measured, PixelLab profile vs LimeZu profile: barn_dog 49x42 vs feralDog 46x40 (+7% / +5%); infected_hog 61x39 vs sickHog 54x32 (+13% / +22%); infected_sheep 58x54 vs blownSheep 52x36 (+12% / +50%); whitacre_bull 64x43 vs prizeBull 92x26 (-30% / +65%).

SO THE MISMATCH IS CAMERA ANGLE, NOT SCALE. Widths already agree within ~13% for dog, hog and sheep. Heights do not, because PixelLab drew these nearly side-on where LimeZu draws its animals from a high top-down -- LimeZu's prizeBull profile is 92 wide by 26 tall, a cow foreshortened from above, against a bull standing at 64x43. Scaling to match height would leave them too narrow. Do not solve this with a scale factor.

START WITH barn_dog. At +7% wide and +5% tall against the feralDog already on the field it is the one animal that is effectively a drop-in, and it is a weapon minion rather than an enemy, so a wrong call costs one summon and not the enemy roster. Wire it, look at it next to a feral dog in a real run, and let that settle whether the remaining nine need a re-generation at LimeZu's camera height.

STILL A JUDGEMENT, NOT A MEASUREMENT: four directions or eight. The renderer buckets an enemy's velocity into four; going to eight is a change there, not in the art. Four ships sooner and wastes half of what was generated. Nothing measured above decides this.
Then: a sprites.json group, npm run atlas, and an enemies.json entry pointing at the new keys.

_horrorPlan._note: MAKE THE WHOLE CAST SCARY, the way the farmhand already is. The infected farmhand is the one piece of this that is finished and it is the enemy you see most in a run; everything else infected is still an ordinary animal wearing a CSS filter, and it looks like it.
_horrorPlan._whatWorks: The farmhand was made with Characters -> Create from Text, Humanoid, Pro, character size 40 custom, camera Low Top-Down, with limezu_character_ref.png and limezu_style_char_128.png as references, then the Scary Walk 8-frame preset. Full recipe in docs/PIXELLAB.md. Use the FARMHAND ITSELF as the Style Character for everything infected that follows -- that is what makes a cast rather than a collection.
_horrorPlan._order: Do the animals the player meets most first. The infected side views for hen, rooster, hog and sheep are generated and staged; they are references for the 8-direction pass, not shippable enemies.
_horrorPlan._pairing: Every horror version should be generated FROM its healthy counterpart as a reference image, so the two read as the same animal before and after. That is the whole horror premise of the game and it does not survive generating them independently.
_horrorPlan._theToolIsCreateObjectState: SOLVED, and this is the tool: create_object_state(object_id, edit_description) takes a finished 8-direction object, applies the edit and returns a NEW object with all eight rotations intact. That is the pairing requirement above, satisfied by construction — the cursed animal is literally derived from the healthy one. About 30-90s each and they can be fired ten at a time.
_horrorPlan._nameTheColourNotTheSymptoms: THE LESSON, and it explains why session 9's infected livestock 'came back only mildly diseased'. An edit that only ADDS detail is resisted by the base image; an edit that RESTATES THE BASE COLOUR replaces it. 'matted patchy coat, ribs showing, green staining' left the white fjord pony pure white and the brown barn dog friendly and brown. 'the whole white coat turned filthy grey-green and diseased, fur sloughing away in bald patches showing raw grey skin beneath' worked on the retry for both. Dark animals curse easily because the disease palette is already near their coat; pale ones have to be told to change colour.
_horrorPlan._cursedStaged: Generated, downloaded to assets/pixellab/object/<name>/, NOT packed: bull_cursed, donkey_cursed, arabian_cursed, draft_mule_cursed (all four strong, first try), plus fjord_pony_cursed2 and barn_dog_cursed2 (the retries, after the colour lesson above — the first attempts are kept as *_cursed and are NOT usable). Each has 8 rotations and no animation yet; animate_object(mode='v3') is 1 generation per direction if they need to walk.

_mapsAndTilesets._note: OWNER WANTS MORE MAPS. Logged to think through before generating, because this is the first thing on the list that changes the GAME rather than the art.
_mapsAndTilesets._whatTheSeedActuallyDoes: Right now the seed drives enemy spawns, elite rolls, drops, offer-pool draws and crop scatter -- everything that goes through the mulberry32 RNG. It does NOT pick a map, because there is one arena: a flat terrain bake with crop nodes scattered on it. Same ground every run. So "maps spawn randomly on the seed" is not true yet; making it true is a real feature, not a content drop.
_whatItWouldTake: A map descriptor in content: tileset, ground bake, node mix, hazard flavour, arena size.
The terrain bake reading that descriptor instead of the one hardcoded set.
The seed choosing a map, which means the map choice must be the FIRST draw off the RNG -- anything else and adding a map silently changes every existing seed replay.
A test that the same seed still replays identically, which is a non-negotiable in this project.
_mapsAndTilesets._generationSide: PixelLab does have the tools for this: create_topdown_tileset for whole ground sets, create_path_tiles for tracks and dirt roads, create_map_object for props, and animate_object for the twinkle. An animated gem seam or a plant that moves is exactly what create_object_state / animate_object are for, and it would make a harvest node read as worth standing on before you commit to standing there -- which is the mining design already in place.
_mapIdeas: the home quarter at dusk (what exists)
the blighted field, dead trees and ash
the creek bottom, water and mud that slows
the night pasture, lit only by burn barrels
_mapsAndTilesets._doFirst: SUPERSEDED by the owner, who asked for tiles BEFORE more maps: 'lets generate a bunch of tiles so the floor can be more detailed and not so blocky'. Six sets are generated and staged in assets/tilesets/ (PNG + metadata). The caution it carried still half-applies -- they have nowhere to go until the terrain bake can read a Wang set -- but the ground is the largest surface on screen and it was the thing actually complained about.

_tilesetRecipe._note: SETTINGS MATTER MORE THAN THE PROMPT, and the first three attempts were unusable because of them.
_tilesetRecipe.use: detail='low detail', shading='flat shading', outline='lineless', text_guidance_scale=15, tile_size 32.
_tilesetRecipe._why: At 32px 'highly detailed' does not mean more texture, it means more STRUCTURE, and structure on a ground tile is a repeating pattern you can count -- it returned tan paving with a purple grid for 'dry cracked dirt', and grey dungeon cobblestone for 'blighted ash-grey dead earth'. 'selective outline' puts a hard dark rule around every terrain edge, which IS the blockiness being complained about; lineless is the single most important setting. Guidance 15 over the default 8 is what makes it draw the terrain asked for rather than a generic one. Short concrete descriptions beat long evocative ones.
_tilesetRecipe._chaining: Pass a finished set's `upper` base tile id as the next set's `lower_base_tile_id` and the two share that terrain EXACTLY. All the staged sets hang off one grass (6e1d7fea-bdf8-4bc7-b1ac-5bae783bf694), so grass->soil, grass->ash and grass->water all meet the same field.
_tilesetRecipe._toWireIt: The bake draws one sprite per cell; a Wang set means choosing a tile from its FOUR CORNER VALUES. That is a real change in renderer.ts. Slice with each tile's `bounding_box` from the metadata -- the API warns that `wang_N` and `original_position` are NOT sheet positions and using them produces horizontal banding.

_classifierNote: A generation request for the Boot Knife was once refused by the CLAUDE CODE permission classifier -- the agent harness, not PixelLab. The prompt never reached the API. Retrying the identical request went straight through and returned sixteen good knives. If a generation is refused, check WHICH layer refused it before rewriting the prompt: the wording was never the problem.

_musicTodo._what: Three CC-0 tracks by Abstraction from the Music Loop Bundle. See src/content/audio.json.
_musicTodo._oggNotMp3: The pack author warns that MP3 will not loop seamlessly -- the format leaves a short gap at the loop point. Every layer loops for as long as a wave lasts, so that gap would be audible dozens of times a run. The loader takes its filename from content, so this was a JSON change with no code change at all.
_musicTodo._leftToDo: Listen to them in a real run. They were chosen from the pack's own metadata -- tags, energy, duration, the author's own score -- and by reading, not by ear. The choice of a 64s ambient spooky bed for the field and an 85s dnb for combat is a judgement that should be checked against actual play.

_licenceRule: THE REPO IS PUBLIC, so committing a pack to assets/ IS redistribution -- the exact deadlock that kept this repo private through M0-M5 until LimeZu gave written permission. Almost every itch.io pack forbids redistribution while allowing use in a project. If one is ever wanted: gitignore its assets/ subfolder. The atlas and public/audio/ are already generated and gitignored, so the build output ships (which those licences allow) and nothing licensed enters the public repo. The cost is that a fresh clone cannot rebuild without the packs on disk.

_eightDirNotes.tool: create_8_direction_object, 20 generations, about four minutes, returns eight rotation URLs rather than a sheet. "npm run object -- <name> <url-prefix>" pulls them down and writes a _ring.png with all eight side by side on grey. JUDGE THE RING, never a single frame: the failure mode is one direction that does not belong to the same animal as the other seven, and that is invisible one frame at a time.
_eightDirNotes.identity: The tool warns that reference identity transfer is unreliable for CHARACTER sprites. It held perfectly for all ten ANIMALS -- every ring is recognisably the same animal as the side view it was generated from. Do not extrapolate to humanoids; the docs say use create_character (mode=v3) for those.
_eightDirNotes.size: Output size comes from the reference image and cannot be set alongside it. Ours came back 56-68px. The game's existing LimeZu animals measure 46-54px wide and 32-40px TALL, so these are noticeably taller -- they stand upright where LimeZu's are drawn at a flatter top-down angle. Stand one next to a pig before committing them to the field.
_eightDirNotes.transitBug: reference_image_base64 IS INTERMITTENTLY TRUNCATED IN TRANSIT. The error says "broken data stream" and reports the full byte count, so it reads like a corrupt file when it is not -- the same file opens fine in PIL locally. It is NOT size-related: 814, 1424, 1938 and 2149 byte payloads succeeded while 1365, 2098 and 3898 byte ones failed, and one file failed twice then succeeded unchanged. JUST RETRY. Re-encoding through PIL, or quantising to the LimeZu palette, shortens the payload and makes a retry likelier to land -- and quantising conforms the art on the way in as a bonus.
_eightDirNotes.horrorNote: The four infected rings came back only mildly diseased -- the hog reads as a spotted pig and the sheep as an ordinary sheep in grey. They are not frightening. The prompts carried the horror ("diseased", "red eyes", "matted") and the model mostly ignored it in favour of the reference. Getting a genuinely horrific cast is a direction problem, not a throughput one.
_eightDirNotes.animation: animate_object(mode="v3") costs ONE generation per direction -- eight for a full ring, against 160-320 for mode="pro". Measured, not read: balance went 451 to 443 across one animal. It queues one job per direction, so a single call consumes the whole 8-job concurrency limit and animals have to be animated one at a time, about four minutes each.
_eightDirNotes.download: "npm run object -- <object-id> <name>" pulls the whole object as a zip from /mcp/objects/<id>/download -- rotations and every animation frame in named folders -- and writes _ring.png plus a _walk_<dir>.png strip per direction. The zip is read in-process rather than shelled out: this machine's tar is GNU tar, which does not read zips at all, and whether `unzip` exists varies. Zip's central directory is forty lines to walk and the entries are raw-deflated, which Node's zlib already does for the PNG codec.
